## What was proved

The central result is a sharp six-player theorem for singleton-normalized exact cooperative games:

\[
s(6)=\sup_v\frac{\|L_{\min}(v)-L_{\max}(v)\|_1}{v(N)}=\frac23.
\]

That contains both halves:

- Universal upper bound: every exact six-player game satisfies normalized \(L_1\) separation at most \(2/3\).
- Sharpness: the explicit game \(G(2,3)\) attains exactly \(2/3\).

So this is not merely a computational lower bound, a large finite experiment, or “verified for many games.” It determines the exact extremal value for the entire six-player domain, conditional on the proof’s human-to-machine reduction being correct.

A secondary result classifies the equality payoff profiles: up to relabeling, only two \(L_{\min},L_{\max}\) profile types attain the bound.

The key is a two-sided Lehman interpolation. For
\[
F_d=(r-p)w_d+p-\ell-(r-\ell)u_d,
\]
the proof excludes both
\[
0\le F_d\le k(r-\ell)
\quad\text{and}\quad
-k(r-p)\le F_d\le0,
\]
by normalizing the gaining or losing poor-player load respectively. Lehman regularity also yields
\[
\sum_dF_d=k(\ell-p)>0.
\]

For any projective plane, a point exists on exactly one gaining line. Its residual automatically falls into one of those two forbidden bands, regardless of the plane’s order or whether it is Desarguesian.

## What we were doing

Cooperative game theory studies how to fairly split the profits of a team when different sub-groups could make different amounts on their own. A "solution" is a rule that outputs one split (the most famous is the **nucleolus**). A basic fairness question about any rule is **monotonicity**: if a group's earning power goes up, no member of that group should get *less*. It sounds obvious — and it's famously false for most rules, which is why the field cares exactly where it holds and where it breaks.
